doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Award shows and sidelining in films
summary: Shear describes AFI award shows, miming to pre-recorded tracks, and sidelining in films like Brewster's Millions.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Like give me an example. What kind of show would that have been?

Well I did — oh just so many things — The American Film Institute awards, where they honor somebody every year for their work, like Jack Lemmon I did and people like that. And a lot of times they would go to commercial especially and you’d make believe you’re playing, which is already recorded.

You know it’s funny you say that because I don’t watch those shows a lot but sometimes I’d watch them, and they would announce a winner or something and boom, immediately — and I’m thinking how do the guys shuffle their music so fast?
Well we know in advance who’s going to get an award.

Well the conductor does, and he’ll call a tune out. And you can figure it out from the music that you’re going to play. So sometimes it is actually — and we do play. But other times it’s sort of pantomiming to what we already recorded. It’s us on tape. Yeah. Same thing in movies when you see musicians in a scene and they’re playing. They’re not really playing. I’ve done a lot of that.
You’ve done a lot of that?

Yeah. Yeah. Oh movies like The Mae West Story and PeeWee’s Big Top Adventure or whatever that was, and a lot of movies like that we see live bands. Brewster’s Millions with Richard Pryor, going back to the 80s. They did a lot more of that then. But most of the time we’d get there very early and pre-record ourself. And then we’d just play to our own tracks. Because they don’t want that sound while people are giving dialogue.
Right. They want to have some control.
Absolutely. They want all the control. Which is fine with us you know. It’s work.
Yeah. And you get extra work for being on film, extra bread for being on film.
